rationale: The BOOK ENTRY defines righteousness as right-living — God's commandments lived out by those under His authority, with God Himself as Right-Living by definition and sin as the opposite. The printed proof-texts carry this almost verbatim: Deuteronomy 6:25 ('it shall be our righteousness, if we observe to do all these commandments'), Psalm 119:172 ('all thy commandments are righteousness'), and 1 John 3:7 ('he that doeth righteousness is righteous'), while Deuteronomy 32:4 and Psalm 145:17 ground the claim that God's own ways are the measure of right. The strongest counter — righteousness as a purely forensic, imputed status distinct from conduct — leans on Romans 4:4-8 and Philippians 3:9, both of which the entry deliberately prints and the supporting material answers: Romans 4 contrasts faith with wage-claiming labor (confirmed by Luke 17:7-10, also printed, where even complete obedience earns no wage), and Romans 4:7-8 itself glosses the imputation of righteousness as the non-imputation of sin — matching the entry's 'Opposite: Sin.' Heb 11:8 shows the counted faith of Gen 15:6 acting in obedience. The forensic counter must split the word into two unrelated senses to survive Deut 6:25, Ps 119:172, and 1 John 3:7, and cannot explain Rev 19:8's plural dikaiōmata (righteous acts) invoked by the referenced Garments chapter, whereas the book's 'granted in source, right-living in substance' account explains both text sets without contradiction. Every material assertion actually printed in the entry is supported; hence FULL.
book_core_identification: Righteousness is right-living: for creatures under God's authority, it is God's commandments lived out; God Himself is Right-Living by definition (His own ways being the standard); its opposite is sin.
book_secondary_elaborations: God is Right-Living by definition (He obeys no superior; His ways are the measure of right — Deut 32:4; Ps 145:17).
The scope qualifier 'for those under His authority' — the commandment-keeping definition applies to creatures, not to God as an obeyer of commands.
The stated opposite: Sin (consistent with 1 John 3:4's 'sin is the transgression of the law' and Rom 4:7-8's non-imputation of sin).
chapter_only_objections: The Garments chapter's claim that the KJV's 'righteousness of saints' in Rev 19:8 built 'a long confusion' folding sanctification into justification is a polemical historical claim not asserted in the entry.
The identification of the bath in John 13:10 with baptism, and feet-washing as daily cleansing of conduct, is a chapter-level typology.
The helmet-of-salvation-as-Yeshuah/Name derivation and the 'whole armour = symbolic vocabulary of Scripture' claim are chapter-level constructions.

The End of the Law's specific applications (Colossians 2 sabbath/feast reading, Romans 14 as koinos-food dispute, Galatians 4 as pagan calendar) are contested chapter arguments beyond the glossary definition.
The reinterpretation of Isaiah 64:6 (filthy rags as stained by the doer's sin rather than works being worthless) is a chapter-level exegesis.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Classic Protestant imputed forensic righteousness: righteousness, in its decisive soteriological sense, is a legal status — right standing before God — credited to the believer by faith apart from works (Rom 4:5-6; Phil 3:9), a declared verdict rather than conduct; ethical uses of the word (Deut 6:25; 1 John 3:7) are a distinct secondary sense, so righteousness should be defined primarily as conferred standing, not as commandments lived out.
counter_core_identification: Righteousness is fundamentally a conferred legal standing before God — Christ's righteousness credited to the believer by faith — not the believer's own commandment-keeping conduct.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that righteousness is, in substance, commandments lived out; it asserts the term's controlling referent is a declared status that exists apart from and prior to any conduct, so the same word cannot be defined as right-living.
counter_case: Romans 4:5-6 says God 'imputeth righteousness without works' to the one who 'worketh not, but believeth' — righteousness credited apart from doing.
Philippians 3:9 opposes 'mine own righteousness, which is of the law' to 'the righteousness which is of God by faith,' apparently disqualifying law-keeping as the definition.
Genesis 15:6 pattern: faith itself, not obedience, is counted for righteousness.
Isaiah 64:6 (in the common interpretation's basis) calls human righteousnesses filthy rags, suggesting conduct cannot constitute righteousness before God.
book_explanatory_advantages: Deut 6:25 and Ps 119:172 state the entry's definition nearly verbatim; the counter must demote these to a separate, secondary sense of the same word.

1 John 3:7 explicitly warns against defining righteousness apart from doing ('let no man deceive you: he that doeth righteousness is righteous'), a warning the book's definition honors and the forensic-only counter must deflect.

Rom 4:7-8 defines the imputation by David's forgiveness — sin not imputed — which coheres with the entry's 'Opposite: Sin' and with imputation as restored standing rather than a redefinition of the word righteousness.

Luke 17:7-10, printed with the entry, supplies the wage-vs-duty key: Romans 4 excludes works as wage-claims, not obedience as the substance of righteousness, so the book reads Rom 4 without making Paul contradict Rom 3:31 ('we establish the law') or 6:16 ('obedience unto righteousness').
Rev 19:8's dikaiōmata (righteous acts of the saints, granted and worn) unifies the 'given' texts with the 'done' texts under one definition: granted in source, right-living in substance.
Heb 11:8 shows the paradigm believer of Gen 15:6 believing by obeying, tying counted faith to enacted faithfulness.
The definition covers God's own righteousness (Deut 32:4; Ps 145:17) without strain: His ways are the standard of right-living itself.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Reads Rom 4:5-6 and Phil 3:9 at maximal face value: righteousness is credited to the non-worker, and Paul explicitly disowns law-derived righteousness.
Aligns with the dominant Protestant doctrinal tradition and its systematic account of justification.
Explains why righteousness can be possessed by the ungodly at the moment of believing, before any conduct exists.
decisive_sources: Romans 4:4-8 read with Luke 17:7-10 (wage/duty distinction) and Rom 4:7-8's forgiveness gloss
Deuteronomy 32:4 and Psalm 145:17 for God's righteousness
Revelation 19:8 (dikaiōmata) via the referenced Garments chapter
unresolved_objections: Phil 3:9's stark 'not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law' remains the counter's strongest single verse; the book's source-vs-substance resolution (granted, then worn) is coherent and cross-supported but is an inference rather than an explicit statement of that verse.

Gen 15:6/Rom 4:5 count faith itself as righteousness at a point before works; the entry accommodates this as righteousness granted in source, but the entry's one-line definition does not itself articulate the granting mechanism.
